The

What it is, who made it, and how the decoder takes input to output — one stage at a time.

Decoder walkthrough
We'll open with what a Transformer is and who invented it, show the full decoder architecture, then walk through the decoder stage by stage.

First things first

What is a Transformer?

The short answer

A Transformer is a type of neural network built to understand and generate sequences — text, code, images, audio.

Its core idea is attention: every element decides which other elements matter most to it.

Two halves

  • Encoders — understand text (BERT)
  • Decoders — generate text (GPT)

This talk focuses on the decoder — the part that powers chatbots and text generation.

Intro
A Transformer is a sequence model based on attention. There are encoders and decoders. We cover the decoder.

Origin

Who made the Transformer?

📄

"Attention Is All You Need"

Published in 2017 at NeurIPS.

Google Brain, Google Research, University of Toronto.

Intro
Introduced in 2017 by a Google-led team. The title says it all: attention alone, no recurrence.

Roadmap of the decoder pipeline. Each stage gets its own slide from here.

Stage 1

Tokenization

The model never sees raw text. This stage chops the input into small pieces called tokens and maps each one to a number from a fixed vocabulary.

Input"The cat sat"
Output[482, 8421, 3390]
The cat sat
The
cat
sat
482
8421
3390
text → tokens → vocabulary IDs
Tokenization converts text to a list of integer IDs the model can process. Unknown words are split into sub-word pieces.

Stage 2

Embeddings

Each token ID is replaced by a fixed-length list of numbers — its coordinates in "meaning space." Words with similar meanings sit near each other. These positions are learned during training.

Input[482, 8421, 3390]
Output3 meaning vectors

The
8421
cat
3390
sat
token IDs → learned meaning vectors
Embeddings map each token to a dense vector whose position encodes meaning. The model learns these positions from data.

Stage 3

Positional Encoding

The decoder reads every token at once, so it has no built-in sense of order. This stage adds a unique "position stamp" to each embedding so the model knows where each token sits.

Inputmeaning vectors
Outputvectors + position

Embedding

Position

Combined
a unique position number is stamped onto each token, then added to its embedding
Positional encoding injects order information into each embedding so the model can distinguish "dog bites man" from "man bites dog".

Stage 4

Masked Self-Attention

Each token looks at the tokens before it to gather context — but never at tokens that come after. The "mask" blocks the future so the model learns to predict honestly.

Inputordered vectors
Outputcontext-aware vectors
The
cat
sat
on
mat

"sat" attends to The & cat (past). Future tokens are masked.

Masked self-attention is the decoder's signature. Each token can see only previous tokens. This is what makes generation work — you can't peek at the answer.

Stage 5

Multi-Head Attention

Attention runs several times in parallel — each "head" looks for a different kind of relationship (grammar, reference, topic). Their results are then merged into one.

Inputcontext vectors
Outputmerged, richer vectors
Head 1
Head 2
Head 3
↓
MERGED OUTPUT
parallel attention heads → combined
Multiple attention heads run in parallel, each capturing a different relationship, then their outputs are concatenated and projected together.

Stage 6

Feed-Forward Network

After words share information via attention, each token is processed independently. This is where the model does its main "thinking" — transforming each vector based on what it learned.

Inputone vector
Outputrefined vector
→
FFN
→
each vector passes through a shared two-layer network
The feed-forward network applies the same transformation to every position independently. It's the "compute" step; attention was the "communicate" step.

Stage 7

Residual Connection

After attention or feed-forward, the original input is added back to the result. This guarantees nothing is lost and lets very deep stacks train successfully.

Inputvector
Outputvector + processed copy
INPUT
x
process
(attention / FFN)
skip (x)
+
OUTPUT
x + f(x)
original + processed = output
Residual connections add the input back to the output of a sub-layer. They preserve information and make deep networks trainable.

Stage 8

Layer Normalization

Before each major step, the numbers in each vector are rescaled to a consistent range. This keeps training stable — nothing gets too loud or too quiet.

Inputuneven vector
Outputleveled vector

values rescaled to a steady range

Layer normalization standardizes the values in each vector, stabilizing training and allowing faster convergence. It's applied before attention and before feed-forward.

The Decoder Block

Stages 4–8 fit into one repeatable block: masked attention → add & norm → feed-forward → add & norm. This is the unit the decoder stacks.

one decoder block — repeated N times
The decoder block chains masked attention, residual+norm, feed-forward, residual+norm. This is the fundamental repeating unit.

Depth

Stack the Block N Times

The decoder block is repeated many times (12 to 128). The output of one block feeds into the next. Each layer refines the representation a little more, building deeper understanding.

Inputvectors
Outputdeep context vectors

Decoder Block 1
⋮
output flows upward through the stack
Stacking many blocks lets the model build increasingly abstract representations. Each layer adds a level of processing.

Stage 9

Output Head

The final vector (from the last position) is mapped to a score for every word in the vocabulary. The highest-scoring word becomes the model's prediction.

Inputfinal context vector
Outputnext token

vocabulary scores → pick the tallest

A linear layer projects the final hidden state to the full vocabulary size, producing a score per token. The token with the highest score is chosen (or sampled).

Stage 10

Autoregressive Loop

To produce more than one word, the model repeats: predict a token, append it to the input, run again. This cycle continues until the model emits a stop signal.

Inputcurrent sequence
Outputsequence + 1 token
Input
→
Predict
→
Append
↻

repeat until the END token

Generation is autoregressive: each new token is conditioned on all previous ones. The loop stops at an end-of-sequence token or a length limit.
